pr_body:
Fixes #12224 

New KeyType `KeyTypePrincipal` and struct `PrincipalKey` is created.
It's reusing the `PublicKey` table, changes are:
- content/name is the same
- fingerprint is empty
- has `KeyTypePrincipal`
- creates `authorized_principals` file instead of `authorized_keys`

`PublicKey` is modified so it doesn't write KeyTypes with `KeyTypePrincipal` to the authorized_keys.

New section is added to the SSH / GPG keys section.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1810977/87951395-cf551e80-caa8-11ea-98f7-344db6b2361d.png)

The `sshd_config` is also modified by adding a `AuthorizedPrincipalsFile` managed by gitea and a `TrustedUserCAKeys` pointing to `/data/ssh/trusted-user-ca-keys.pem` which should be managed by the gitea administrator. (this contains the publickey of the CA that signs your ssh certificates)

Updates to the original PR:
- built-in ssh server supported
- `SSH_TRUSTED_USER_CA_KEYS` option has been added to the config for specifying your CA keys (and have gitea manage them)
- `SSH_TRUSTED_USER_CA_KEYS_FILENAME` has been added to the config for specifying the filename gitea will manage the CA keys in
- Extra `SSH_AUTHORIZED_PRINCIPALS_ALLOW` has been added to config which by default only allows principals that are equal 
to the user's email or username (to avoid malicious activity). Option to allow anything is also available
- Option to update the authorized principals file has been added to the admin dashboard (like the authorized keys file)

> * Why didn't you add a KeyTypePrincipalDeploy? Or do you think that the certificate route makes these unnecessary?

Certificates are normally short-lived, imo it wouldn't make sense to use them for deploy keys, which are mostly used in CI/CD or scripts.

> * We really can't just obliterate the old certificate.pem file - we need to somehow provide an option to do it or some way of appending to it. <- THIS IS A BLOCKER FOR THIS PR

This problem must be seen in two different setups, using the docker image and using it without docker.

### Using docker

To be sure of clashes with an existing `~/git/.ssh/trusted-ca-keys.pem` (of which the changes are really slim) we can rename it to `44720ad3-c02b-40e4-9b3a-5e3d37e33cc0-trusted-ca-keys.pem`. This makes sure that we're the one managing it.

### Outside docker

In the real world no-one would actually put the `trusted-ca-keys.pem` in ~/git/.ssh. They would already have a `trusted-ca-keys.pem` in like `/etc/ssh/trusted-ca-keys.pem` and would not let gitea manage that.

So what about adding an extra option `SSH_TRUSTED_USER_CA_KEYS_FILE` which by default is `SSH.RootPath/44720ad3-c02b-40e4-9b3a-5e3d37e33cc0-trusted-user-ca-keys.pem`. 

This way we're sure we are the ones managing it (which works in the docker scenario above) and if they actually want to use the gitea generated file they change their `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` to have `TrustedUserCAKeys` pointed to `SSH.RootPath/44720ad3-c02b-40e4-9b3a-5e3d37e33cc0-trusted-user-ca-keys.pem`.

> Sorry I misunderstood how this is supposed to work - I see now that these principals are just usernames/email-addresses. I guess the CA is responsible for checking who gets those principals - however what's to stop a malicious user from adding your principal name to their account before you can get it? That way they could catch your private pushes.

It works the same as the public key, it has the same issues when the malicious user would add your public key to their account before you can get it. 

The SSH certificates basically works as follows: you have a SSH CA somewhere (eg via hashicorp vault), this SSH CA signs your public key and this certificate will contain the principals (that you are allowed to/want to use) and returns you a ssh certificate containing a few things, the specified principals (if you had access to those, normally this is a username) and a specific lifetime.

When you know give this certificate to sshd, it'll check:
- if you own the private key used for this certificate
- if the lifetime is valid
- if it was signed by the correct SSH CA
- and if the principal exists somewhere in the `authorized_principals` file.

The SSH CA part / signing is something done outside of gitea, just like the creating of the public/private keys is.

For a follow-up PR, it'd like to add an option for a `default` principal, the gitea admin can specify for example, each user will be linked to a principal equal to its username, or email etc..

Thanks for this PR, I'm trying to test this however I am new to using SSH certificates. Could you provide a brief getting started on using SSH certificates in Gitea?

@techknowlogick  quick tutorial, normally you would use something as vault in production for managing this stuff.

This example is using the gitea built-in ssh server

## generate ssh-ca used for signing

```
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C ssh-ca -f ssh-ca
Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Your identification has been saved in ssh-ca.
Your public key has been saved in ssh-ca.pub.
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:bOBEoJxWWRAQVdwNxWpjfHxRbfCBLbCEhDJKLA3YtR8 ssh-ca
The key's randomart image is:
+--[ED25519 256]--+
|.o*=BO+.+*oo..=+ |
|.o.B.=....+ oo o+|
|  B o E. o . ....|
| . . + +* o .    |
|      ooSo .     |
|       .         |
|                 |
|                 |
|                 |
+----[SHA256]-----+
```

## put the ca public key in gitea config
```
$ cat ssh-ca.pub
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIDAwkb1+7mK5BnwWXxl8Flh3mG716I0eXfhDBc9TOEzn ssh-ca
```

So in your gitea `app.ini` put

`SSH_TRUSTED_USER_CA_KEYS = ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIDAwkb1+7mK5BnwWXxl8Flh3mG716I0eXfhDBc9TOEzn ssh-ca`

restart gitea

## generate your own sshkey that will be used for authentication

(No password for quick testing, obviously do not do this in production)

```
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N ''  -f mykey
Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Your identification has been saved in mykey.
Your public key has been saved in mykey.pub.
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:5ac8VPYwb6MYu5WharbN/hIjWRe7Xu51XhXw1Xu2sYM wim@server
The key's randomart image is:
+--[ED25519 256]--+
|             .  o|
|            . o o|
|          . =o o.|
|         o.oo= o+|
|        So+.o.*.*|
|        oooB.E.=.|
|         .B++o  =|
|        o+.+. .oo|
|       ooo=o... .|
+----[SHA256]-----+
```

## sign this sshkey with the ssh-ca 

with principal `wim` and a lifetime of 1 hour

```
$ ssh-keygen -s ssh-ca -I keyid -n wim -V -5:+1h -z 1 mykey.pub
Signed user key mykey-cert.pub: id "keyid" serial 1 for wim valid from 2020-08-29T13:59:05 to 2020-08-29T14:59:10
```

## start an ssh-agent

$ eval `ssh-agent`
Agent pid 42183

## add the key and certificate to your agent

```
$ ssh-add mykey
Identity added: mykey (wim@server)
Certificate added: mykey-cert.pub (keyid)
```

`ssh-add -l` should show them both

```
$ ssh-add -l
256 SHA256:5ac8VPYwb6MYu5WharbN/hIjWRe7Xu51XhXw1Xu2sYM wim@server (ED25519)
256 SHA256:5ac8VPYwb6MYu5WharbN/hIjWRe7Xu51XhXw1Xu2sYM wim@server (ED25519-CERT)
```

## in gitea add the principal `wim` to your account

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1810977/91636650-8aef6380-ea02-11ea-90c2-a7a51983ea99.png)

## now clone from your gitea instance

Just use git clone and you should be able by using your certificate.

```
git clone git@yourserver:youruser/yourproject.git
```

@zeripath I've added a commit that should fix your security comments (as discussed on discord too)

This commit adds a `SSH_AUTHORIZED_PRINCIPALS_ALLOW` option which is default
`email,username` this means that users only can add the principals
that match their email or username.

To allow anything the admin need to set the option `anything`.

This allows for a safe default in gitea which protects against malicious
users using other user's prinicipals. (before that user could set it).

This commit also has some small other fixes from the last code review.

@zeripath 
This won't work

```
AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand /path/to/gitea keys-principal -e git -u %u -i %i
```
the `%i` is the ssh certificate keyid, it's not the principals themselves, this key id isn't in gitea (it's something the ssh-ca generates).


The right way I think is to do this:
```
AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand /path/to/gitea keys-principal -e git -u %u
```

And have it spit out all the `KeyTypePrincipals` for that specific user, because all those are valid.

issue_context.title: Proposal: support ssh certificates
issue_context.body:
## Description

Support [ssh certificates](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/master/PROTOCOL.certkeys)

This way users can get access without uploading a public ssh key, instead they are verified against a ssh CA.

This will need extra sshd configuration like this

```
AuthorizedPrincipalsFile .ssh/authorized_principals
TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/trusted-user-ca-keys.pem
```

`.ssh/authorized_principals` basically need to output the same as the authorized_keys file eg

```
command="/app/gitea/gitea serv key-1 --config='/data/gitea/conf/app.ini'",no-port-forwarding,no-X11-forwarding,no-agent-forwarding,no-pty principal
```

The difference is the `principal` instead of the ssh key, this should match the valid principals in your ssh certificate. 

In our case this will match with the usernames in gitea.

In the GUI there should be an option for a user to:
- activate this feature 
- maybe specify the principal that should be matched (default username)

In the configfile, there should be an option to specify the system-wide CA (the contents of `/etc/ssh/trusted-user-ca-keys.pem`)

It's possible to fit this in the `public_key` table by putting the correct principal in the `content` field instead of the ssh-key

I'm prepared to work on this.
